161.explanation: In the Sidh Gosht, his dialogue with the yogis, Guru Nanak describes the Gurmukh, the person oriented to the Guru, as one whose way of life clears hatred and envy out of the heart.
161.tie_back: The Kural asks us to make a heart free of envy the very rule of conduct; Guru Nanak makes freedom from envy a defining mark of the Gurmukh's way of living.
161.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 942, Raag Raamkalee, Sidh Gosht, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
161._accuracy_note: Strong thematic fit: both make the absence of envy part of the ideal person's settled character; the Kural's pun on right conduct versus the soiled path has no equivalent.

162.quote_or_event: “I have totally forgotten my jealousy of others, … No one is my enemy, and no one is a stranger. I get along with everyone.”
162.explanation: Guru Arjan says that in the company of the holy (the Saadh Sangat) all jealousy of others fell away, so that no one remained an enemy or a stranger to him.
162.tie_back: The Kural prizes being free of envy toward anyone at all above every other gain; Guru Arjan describes exactly that universal release, with envy gone toward everyone.
162.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1299, Raag Kaanraa, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
162._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one on universal freedom from envy; the ellipsis omits one unverified connecting line, and the Kural's claim that this outranks every other gain is implied, not stated.

163.quote_or_event: “Give up your envy of others, you fool!”
163.explanation: Guru Arjan calls envy of other people plain foolishness and tells the mind to drop it, since it profits nothing in a short human life.
163.tie_back: The Kural says the man who envies another's prosperity in effect rejects his own virtue and wealth; Gurbani likewise treats envy as self-defeating folly.
163.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 889, Raag Raamkalee, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
163._accuracy_note: Reasonable but partial: both call envy foolish and self-harming, but the verse does not spell out the Kural's point that the envier gives up his own virtue and prosperity.

164.quote_or_event: “Jealousy and envy bring terrible pain, and one is cursed throughout the three worlds.”
164.explanation: In a salok in Maaroo ki Vaar, Guru Nanak warns that envy brings deep suffering and spoils a person everywhere.
164.tie_back: The Kural's wise person avoids envy-driven wrong because he knows the suffering it brings; Guru Nanak names that suffering plainly.
164.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1091, Raag Maaroo (Maaroo ki Vaar, salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
164._accuracy_note: Strong fit on the pain that envy brings; the Kural's stress on the wise acting from that knowledge is implied rather than stated in the verse.

165.quote_or_event: “In jealousy, the body is not at peace; without the Fear of God, multitudes are ruined.”
165.explanation: In the Dakhni Oankar Guru Nanak teaches that jealousy destroys a person's peace from within, and that those without reverence for God are brought to ruin.
165.tie_back: The Kural says envy alone is enough to ruin a man even if his enemies fail; Guru Nanak likewise places the destruction inside the envious person himself.
165.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 933, Raag Raamkalee, Dakhni Oankar, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
165._accuracy_note: Strong thematic fit on envy as a self-acting cause of ruin; the Kural's contrast with enemies who fail to harm is absent, and some Sikh commentators read the Gurmukhi word as burning desire more broadly.

166.quote_or_event: “The True Lord and Master is on the side of the True Guru; and so, all those who oppose Him waste away to death in anger, envy and conflict.”
166.explanation: Guru Ram Das says that people who resented the greatness the Lord had given the Guru could not take it away, and wore themselves out in envy and strife.
166.tie_back: The Kural warns that one who resents what is given to others perishes along with his kin; Guru Ram Das describes the envious who begrudge God's gift to another wasting themselves away.
166.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 307, Raag Gauree (Gauri ki Vaar), Guru Ram Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
166._accuracy_note: Reasonable but partial: both show envy of what another has been given ending in ruin, but the verse is about opponents of the Guru, and the Kural's picture of kin left without food or clothing is absent.

167.quote_or_event: “All the nine treasures, and the eighteen supernatural powers are held by our Lord and Master in the Palm of His Hand.”
167.explanation: Guru Arjan teaches that all wealth and power rest in the hand of the one God, not with any separate deity of fortune.
167.tie_back: The Kural pictures the goddess of fortune leaving the envious man for her sister Misfortune; Sikh teaching sets aside such goddesses and places all fortune in the One Lord's hand alone.
167.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 10, Rehras (So Dar section), Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
167._accuracy_note: Next-best only: Sikhism does not personify fortune as Lakshmi or misfortune as her elder sister, so this verse answers the Kural's image with a contrast; it says nothing about envy as such.

168.quote_or_event: “In the worlds of Shiva, Brahma and Indra, I wandered around, burning up with envy.”
168.explanation: Guru Arjan describes wandering even through the heavens of the gods while burning with envy, so that even those exalted realms bring no relief.
168.tie_back: The Kural calls envy a matchless sinner that drives a man into the fire of hell; Guru Arjan's image of a soul burning with envy wherever it goes echoes that fire.
168.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1219, Raag Saarang, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
168._accuracy_note: Next-best: the fire image matches, but the verse does not mention envy destroying wealth, and Punjabi commentators (e.g. Sahib Singh) gloss the burning as worldly craving, while Sant Singh Khalsa's translation renders it as envy.

169.quote_or_event: “By His Command, some are high and some are low; by His Written Command, pain and pleasure are obtained.”
169.explanation: In the second pauri of Japji, Guru Nanak teaches that rise and fall, joy and suffering all happen within hukam, the divine order, which is beyond human calculation.
169.tie_back: The Kural asks us to ponder why the envious sometimes prosper and the upright suffer; Japji answers that such reversals of fortune lie within God's hukam.
169.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1, Japji Sahib, Pauri 2, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
169._accuracy_note: Reasonable fit for the theodicy question; the commentators answer the Kural with karma, while Japji answers with hukam (which in Sikh thought also includes karma), and Japji does not single out the envious or the upright.

170.quote_or_event: “One whose heart is filled with jealousy of others, never comes to any good.”
170.explanation: Guru Ram Das states flatly that a heart full of jealousy of others never prospers.
170.tie_back: The Kural closes by saying no one has ever grown great through envy; Guru Ram Das says the envious never come to any good.
170.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 308, Raag Gauree (Gauri ki Vaar), Guru Ram Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
170._accuracy_note: Strong fit for the Kural's first half; its second half, that the envy-free never lose prosperity, is not stated in this verse.
